Efficient fractionation of microalgae biomass as a whole for biodiesel production enabled by deep eutectic solvent and water
Dayong Yu a,b, Hangyu Luo a,b, Jinyu Tan b, Junfa Yuan b, Jiasheng Chen b, Xiaofang Liu a,*, Hu Li b,*

a Guizhou Provincial Key Laboratory for Rare Animal and Economic Insects of the Mountainous Region, College of Biology and Environmental Engineering, Guiyang University, Guiyang 550005, China b National Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide, Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide and Agricultural Bioengineering, Ministry of Education, State-Local Joint Laboratory for Comprehensive Utilization of Biomass, Center for R&D of Fine Chemicals, Guizhou University, Guiyang, 550025, China
ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** Microalgae biomass Deep eutectic solvent Fractionation Microbial lipids

ABSTRACT The fractionation of microalgae biomass and its efficient utilization have always been problems to be solved. Herein, microalgae biomass was pretreated with deep eutectic solvent (DES) to fractionate lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates, which were further converted into biodiesel. DES (CC-LA) synthesized from lactic acid and choline chloride had high fractionation efficiency, and the lipid extraction rate (17.7%) was 2.3 times higher than that of the untreated one (7.7%). Adding 0.5 mol water in CC-LA changed the polarity of the solvent, and the hydrogen bond acidity (α) and hydrogen bond alkalinity (β) increased from 1.37 and 0.52 to 1.42 and 0.54, respectively. Thus, the separation efficiency of DES was significantly improved. The lipid extraction rate was as high as 89.4%, the protein dissolution rate was as high as 84.2%, and the carbohydrate saccharification rate was as high as 96.8%. In addition, the isolated protein and glycosylated carbohydrates could be converted into 8.9 g microbial lipids/100 g microalgae biomass by *Lipomyces starkeyi*. The new water-promoted DES fractionation technology has dramatically enabled microalgae biomass's efficient and comprehensive utilization.

# 1. Introduction Microalgae are unicellular organisms that are easy to culture, can efficiently fix CO2 and reproduce rapidly, and usually contain more than 80% organic matter, such as lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates [1]. These substances are high-quality sources for the preparation of biofuels. Therefore, microalgae are considered the new generation (third generation) of biomass raw materials for biofuel production [2,3]. Biofuels based on microalgae biomass mainly include bioethanol (fermentation of carbohydrates), biodiesel (transesterification of lipids), and biomethane (anaerobic fermentation) [4]. However, the utilization of microalgae biomass faces the problem of low efficiency. Because a large number of available substances are stored in the cytoplasm, the high resistance cell wall of microalgae hinders their effective utilization [5]. In addition, in most cases, only carbohydrates and lipids are used, and a large amount of protein is discharged as waste, resulting in a loss of overall biomass utilization [6]. To address this, it is crucial to develop an efficient and green pretreatment technique to efficiently pretreat and fractionate microalgae biomass (e.g., lipids, carbohydrates, and

The main technical problems for microalgae valorization are the destruction of the microalgae cell wall and the fractionation and utili- zation of total biomass. Currently, pretreatment methods include me- chanical pretreatment (e.g., milling, high-pressure homogenization, microwave, ultrasonication, and pulsed electric field), chemical pre- treatment (e.g., acid, alkali, organic soils, and oxidant), and biological pretreatment (e.g., enzymes and microorganisms) [7,8]. However, several problems are constantly encountered, such as high-energy con- sumption, corrosion of equipment, destruction of the environment, and inability to fractionate microalgae biomass effectively. It is necessary to explore a green and economical pretreatment/fractionation technology. Therefore, many new green solvents have been developed for pretreat- ment, such as ionic liquid (IL), liquid biphasic system (LBS), and deep eutectic solvent (DES).

DES and IL have similar properties, such as non-flammable, non- volatile, recyclable, low vapor pressure, melting point, thermal stability, and so on [9]. However, compared with IL, DES has the advantages of

low cost, simple preparation, non-toxicity, and biodegradability, which makes it more promising [10]. LBS is used for the pretreatment of microalgae biomass, which has cost saving advantages, high separation efficiency, and protein invariance. However, the premise of its practical implementation is the need to destroy the cell wall of microalgae in advance [11]. Studies have shown that DES can effectively destroy the hydrogen bond network on the cell wall of microalgae to achieve the purpose of cracking microalgae cells.

Meanwhile, DES has a high affinity for proteins and can quickly dissolve and extract a large number of proteins during the treatment of microalgae [12]. Significantly, the composition of DES can be freely adjusted to change its physicochemical properties. DES is hydrophilic, and adding an appropriate amount of water can reduce its viscosity and significantly improve its pretreatment performance [13,14]. It is, hence, an excellent choice to prepare suitable DES to pretreat fractionated microalgae biomass.

Upon pretreatment of microalgae biomass with DES, lipids are con-verted into biodiesel by transesterification after extraction, and carbo-hydrates can be converted into biofuels by fermentation. Therefore, the fate of proteins dissolved in the DES phase must be considered. Lip-omyces starkeyi (L. starkeyi) is an excellent oleaginous yeast which pro-duces microbial lipids that can be converted into biodiesel by transesterification [15]. Notably, the substrates required for fermenta-tion are broad-spectrum, including reducing sugars, starch, lignocellu-losic hydrolysates, proteins, and fatty acids [16]. Therefore, the fractionated carbohydrates and proteins in the DES phase can be used as substrates for L. starkeyi to produce microbial lipids, thereby efficiently utilizing whole microalgae biomass. At the same time, it is necessary to consider the toxic effect of DES components on microorganisms during fermentation. Choline chloride-based DES has good biocompatibility and is widely used in biotransformation [17,18]. Therefore, choline chloride (CC) was used as a hydrogen bond acceptor to prepare different DESs in this paper.

To fully utilize microalgae biomass, the concept of "full utilization" for producing biodiesel would be a promising strategy. In this work, a sustainable DES composed of CC and lactic acid (LA) with efficient pretreatment performance was screened out, and the effect of water on the pretreatment performance of the DES was explored. The influences of temperature and time on the optimal DES fractionation efficiency were investigated. After the reaction, the microalgae lipids were obtained by fractionation, and the proteins were fermented as substrates to convert into microbial lipids. The remaining solids (carbohydrates) were enzymatically hydrolyzed into monosaccharides as fermentation substrates, which were also converted into microbial lipids. Finally, the harvested microalgae lipids and microbial lipids were converted into biodiesel. The fractionation and "full utilization" of microalgae biomass components provide a good reference for upgrading biomass to biofuels or value-added chemicals.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Microalgae and chemicals Microalgae powder (_Nannochloropsis_ sp.) was purchased from Shandong Wudi Lvqi Biological Engineering Co., ltd. _Nannochloropsis_ sp. was dried at 105 °C for 48 h to calculate its water content. Carbohydrates, protein, and lipids of microalgae were determined by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL/TP-5100-60957) standard technique [19], Lowry method [20], and Bligh & Dyer method [21], respectively. The content of each component are water 10.5 ± 0.2 %, carbohydrate 15.3 ± 0.4 %, protein 39.2 ± 0.3 %, lipid 30.3 ± 0.6 %, and ash 11.1 ± 0.4 % respectively. The dried microalgae powder was stored in a sealed container and placed in a desiccator for later use. CC (≥99.0 %), formic acid (FA, ≥98.0 %), acetic acid (AA, ≥99.5 %), LA (≥99.0 %), and other chemicals of analytical purity grade were acquired from InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).

## 2.2. Dess synthesis and pretreatment Hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) (i.e., CC) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) (FA, AA, or LA) in a molar ratio of 1:2 were stirred at 80 °C and 600 rpm for 30 min to obtain a clear and transparent colorless liquid, denoted as CC-FA, CC-AA, and CC-LA [12]. For microalgae pretreatment in a typical procedure, CC-LA was added together with 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mol of water. Before use, the prepared DESs were stored in sealed containers and placed in a dryer to avoid absorbing moisture in the air. Typically, a mixture of 0.5 g microalgae powder and 10 g DES was placed in a pressure tube and heated at 600 rpm for pretreatment. The set heating temperature was 80, 100, 120, and 140 °C, and the required time was 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h.

2.3. Extraction of microalgae lipids and enzymatic hydrolysis of residual carbohydrates After pretreatment of microalgae with DES, 20 mL water was added to the reaction system, and then an equal volume of ethyl acetate was added to extract lipids. The upper ethyl acetate was harvested by centrifugation, and the above steps were repeated 3 times. The collected ethyl acetate was combined to remove the solvent by rotary evaporation, and the obtained microalgae lipids were placed at 105 °C to remove water and weighed to calculate the lipid extraction rate. The lipid extraction rate was determined by following the below equation:
Lipid extraction rate (%) = $\frac{\text{Weight of lipid extracted}}{\text{Lipid weight in initial microalgae}}$ \times 100% (1)

The DES aqueous phase was recovered to detect the content of monosaccharides and proteins and used for subsequent fermentation. The remaining solids were douched 3 times with double distilled water (ddH2O) to remove the residual DES and then dried at 105 °C to obtain the recovered microalgae powder (RMP) for subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis.

The enzymatic hydrolysis reaction was evaluated under a 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 4.8) with a solid (raw and RMP) loading of 1% (w/v) and 20 FPU/g solid cellulase (Cellic® CTec2, Filter paper activity: 150 FPU/mL, Novozyme). A final concentration of 50 µg/mL tetracy- cline was then added to inhibit bacterial growth. The system was placed in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask and then hydrolyzed at 200 rpm for 12 h in a preheated (50 °C) shaker. The hydrolysate was taken out at intervals, and the concentration of monosaccharide was determined after the inactivation of the enzyme at 100 °C for 10 min. The concentrations of monosaccharide was detected by HPLC (Agilent 1260, Hi-Plex H, 300 × 7.7 mm, 8 µm) equipped with a differential refractive index detector (RID) with 0.05 mol/L dilute H2SO4 as the mobile phase (0.5 mL/min). The temperature of the column and RID was kept at 50 °C. The mono- saccharide yield was determined following the equation:
Monosaccharide yield (%) = Monosaccharide in the enzymatic liquid (g) / Monosaccharide in the substrate (g) × 100%

## 2.4. Strain and cultivation Lipomyces starkeyi 2.2291 (L. starkeyi), supplied by China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center (CGMCC), was cultured on YPD (yeast peptone dextrose) medium (yeast extract: 10 g/L, tryptone: 20 g/L, glucose: 20 g/L and preparation of solid medium with additional agar: 20 g/L) and stored at 4 °C. The medium was sterilized in an autoclave at 115 °C for 20 min, and the glucose solution was sterilized alone.
The general culture procedure of _L. starkeyi_ includes the following steps. (1) A pure culture of _L. starkeyi_ was obtained according to the

activation procedure provided by CGMCC. (2) The pure culture was inoculated on a YPD solid plate, and a single colony was obtained after 48 h at 28 °C. (3) The single colony was inoculated in a YPD liquid medium, and the enriched pure culture was obtained after 24 h at 28 °C as the initial culture for fermentation.

## 2.5. Fermentation of DES aqueous phase after microalgae pretreatment To test the fermentability of the DES aqueous phase recovered after DES pretreatment of microalgae, L. starkeyi (microbial lipid production by fermentation) was used to evaluate the feasibility. The recovered DES aqueous phase was adjusted to pH 6.0 using solid NaOH, and then 0.5 g/ L MgSO4.7H2O and 1.0 g/L KH2PO4 were added. After sterilization at 121 °C for 20 min, it was used as a medium for L. starkeyi fermentation. The initial culture of L. starkeyi after YPD culture was centrifuged to discard the medium, and the cells were washed with sterile ddH2O 3 times and resuspended, followed by addition to the medium prepared with DES aqueous phase in an inoculation amount of 10% (v/v) so that the cell concentration in the initial fermentation broth was OD600 = 1.0 [22]. Subsequently, the fermentation system (in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask) was cultured in a shaker at 28 °C and 200 rpm for 72 h, and samples were taken every 12 h to determine the consumption of monosaccharides and proteins and the yield of dry cell weight (DCW) and microbial lipid.

2.6. Fermentation of RMP enzymatic hydrolysate To meet the high C/N ratio required for L. starkeyi fermentation, the solid loading for RMP hydrolysis was adjusted to 5 %. The hydrolysate obtained by replacing RMP with untreated, dry microalgae powder was used as a check (CK). 0.5 g/L MgSO4.7H2O, 1.0 g/L KH2PO4, and 0.22 g/ L (NH4)2SO4 were added to the obtained hydrolysate and then sterilized at 121 °C for 20 min and stored in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask. Subsequently, L. starkeyi was inoculated as described in Section 2.5 and fermented at 28 °C and 200 rpm for 72 h. Sampling was performed every 12 h to determine monosaccharide consumption (DCW) and microbial lipid production.

2.7. Lipid extraction After the fermentation broth was harvested, the wet cells were obtained by centrifugation, washed with ddH2O 3 times to remove the residual medium on the cell surface, and then freeze-dried to obtain dry cells. Lipid extraction was performed, according to the published literature [23]. The dry cells were resuspended with 4 M HCl to make the cell suspension concentration (0.1 g/mL). After standing at room temperature for 1 h, it was shaken well again and placed in a water bath at 100 °C for 10 min to lyse the cells fully. Then, an equal volume of methanol and 2 times chloroform were added, fully oscillated, and mixed for 30 min, followed by centrifuging at 8,000 rpm for 5 min. The chloroform layer was recovered, and the same volume of chloroform was added again, repeated 3 times. All chloroform was collected, and the solvent was removed by rotary evaporation. The obtained microbial lipid was dried to constant weight at 105 °C. DCW and lipid yield were determined using equations (3) and (4).
DCW (g/L) = Weight of dried cell / Volume of fermentation medium (3)
Lipid yield (g/L) = Weight of extracted lipid / Volume of fermentation medium
2.8. _Lipid transesterification and fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) composition analysis_

According to previous studies [24], a lipid transesterification reaction was completed in the methanol-sulfuric acid system. Typically, the extracted microalgae and microbial lipids were dissolved in methanol and transferred to a 15 mL pressure tube, then concentrated sulfuric acid was added to a final concentration of 2 % (w/w). The reaction system was placed at 80 °C for 2 h, and an equal volume of ddH2O and an equal volume of ethyl acetate were added to thoroughly mix. Subsequently, the composition of FAME was analyzed by GC-MS (Agilent 6890 N GC, 5973 MS) and GC (Agilent 7890B, HP-5 column: 30 m x 0.32 mm x 0.25 µm, and flame ionization detector) with SUPELCO standard mix as reference.

2.9. *Monosaccharides analytic* After pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and fermentation broth, the monosaccharides in DES aqueous phase were analyzed by HPLC (Agilent 1260, Hi-Plex H, 300 × 7.7 mm, 8 µm). The mobile phase was 50 mM H2SO4 (0.5 mL/min), the detector was RID, and the column temperature and detector temperature were set at 50 °C.

The polarity of the solvent is an important parameter to evaluate its solvation ability, which will affect the reaction rate in the conversion process and its reaction mechanism [30]. Therefore, the solvatochromic probe (dye) of DESs was analyzed by a UV-visible spectrophotometer. K-T parameters usually describe the solvent polarity.. The values of π*, α, and β of the prepared DESs were quantified by N,N-dimethyl-4-nitrobenzene, Nile Red, and 4-nitroaniline dye staining to quantify the dipole/polarizability, hydrogen bond acidity, and hydrogen bond alkalinity, respectively, as shown in Table 1.

The π* values of the synthesized DESs are 1.18 (CC-FA), 0.99 (CC-AA), and 1.16 (CC-LA), respectively. A higher π* value indicates that DES has relatively higher polarizability [31], indicating that the solvents' polarity is in the order of CC-FA > CC-LA > CC-AA. The parameter α reflects the ability of the solvent to provide protons. The α values of DESs studied were between 1.19 and 1.37, with CC-LA showing the highest value (1.37) and CC-AA showing the lowest value (1.19). These

three DESs all exhibit a high α value, that is, the superior ability to provide protons (acidity), considering that the HBDs of the synthesized DESs contain carboxylic acid groups. The parameter β reveals the ability of the solvent to accept protons (forming hydrogen bonds). The β values of the three DESs were basically stable at about 0.50, which were 0.47 (CC-FA), 0.51 (CC-AA), and 0.52 (CC-LA), respectively. However, the β values of these acidic DESs based on CC decreased in the HBD order of LA > AA > FA. The β value of DESs is positively correlated with the length of the HBD alkyl chain.

3.1.2. The fractionation efficiency of DESs on microalgae pretreatment Subsequently, the prepared DESs were used for the pretreatment fractionation of microalgae, and the remaining solid (RMP) after pretreatment was utilized for enzymatic hydrolysis to evaluate the pretreatment effect. The fractionation of each component was shown in Fig. 2 after the pretreatment of microalgae with different DESs at 120 °C for 2 h. Unpretreated microalgae (Raw) only extracted 7.7% lipid. The pretreatment of DESs effectively destroyed the microalgae cells and increased the solubilization of soluble substances (proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids) in microalgae cells. The extraction rate of lipids after pretreatment showed the following order: CC-LA (17.7%) > CC-FA (13.6%) > CC-AA (9.3%). This trend was similar to the concentration of monosaccharides dissolved in liquid. Compared with CC-AA, CC-FA, and CC-LA had relatively higher lipid extraction rates and monosaccharide solubility because they have higher α values. DES with a high α value can release more protons, which can degrade the cell wall network more effectively [32]. The protein concentrations dissolved in the aqueous phase of DESs were 9.5 g/L (CC-FA), 7.1 g/L (CC-AA), and 9.2 g/L (CC-LA), respectively. The extraction rates of lipids (CC-LA > CC-FA > CC-AA) and proteins (CC-FA > CC-LA > CC-AA) by the three DESs were different, depending on their dissolution methods. The extraction efficiency of lipids is determined by the degree of cell damage. The higher the degree of damage, the more conducive to the extraction of ethyl acetate. The polarity and compatibility of the solvent determines the extraction rate of protein. The dissolution trend was consistent with the π* value of DESs, and the solvent with higher polarity contributes to the solubilization of proteins [12]. In general, the fractionation efficiency showed that CC-LA had a better pretreatment effect, followed by CC-FA and CC-AA, which was verified by the saccharification efficiency of RMP (Fig. 2b).

3.1.3. Characterization analysis of RMP RMP was characterized by FT-IR (Fig. 3), showing that DESs effectively destroyed the cell structure of microalgae. The vibration bands around 800–1250 cm⁻¹ and 2800–2950 cm⁻¹ belong to the stretching of polysaccharides [33]. In all pretreated samples, the peak intensity of these regions was significantly improved, especially for CC-LA. This change can be explained by the efficient degradation of the microalgae cell wall network by DESs and more exposure to polysaccharides in the pretreated samples. The destructive effect of microalgae cells can be observed by SEM images of RMP (Fig. 4). Similarly, this exposure effect follows the order of CC-LA > CC-FA > CC-AA. The untreated microalgae cells were round and smooth without damage, while the cells treated with CC-FA and CC-AA showed shrinkage, and a small number of cracks were observed on CC-FA. The most obvious is CC-LA, where microalgae cells appeared with a large number of broken and observed massive cell debris.

As summarized in Table 1, the BET surface area of RMP after DESs pretreatment was higher (0.98–13.02 m²/g) than that of untreated microalgae (0.66 m²/g), which was increased by about 19.7 (CC-LA) times, 2.1 (CC-FA) times, and 1.5 (CC-AA) times, respectively. CC-LA shows a significant increase in surface area related to its higher α and β values. DESs with high α values easily provide hydrogen bonds to release H⁺, while DESs with high β values will show the stronger ability to accept hydrogen bonds [32]. This DES with a high hydrogen supply and absorption capacity is more likely to reduce the hydrogen bond strength between microalgae cell walls, thereby achieving greater cell wall breakage [12]. This is consistent with the surface structure of RMP shown by SEM. The severe destruction of microalgae cells helps to increase the surface area, thereby increasing cellulose accessibility and promoting the saccharification of RMP.

The crystalline properties of RMP were analyzed by XRD (see supplementary information and Table 1). The diffraction pattern of RMP showed a signal similar to that of untreated microalgae, demonstrating that the form of carbohydrates before and after pretreatment did not change [34]. The pretreatment effect of DESs was evaluated by calculating the crystallinity index (CrI). The results showed that the CrI values of RMP components of microalgae biomass pretreated by various DESs increased from 72.3 % to 83.2 %, indicating that the pretreatment process improved the crystallinity of RMP. High crystallinity is closely related to the excellent enzymatic hydrolysis effect [35].

3.3. The effects of CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment temperature and time on microalgae fractionation The above studies have shown that CC-LA-W0.5 has the best pretreatment fractionation effect, so the pretreatment performance of CC-LA-W0.5 at different temperatures and times was further investigated (Fig. 6).
3.3.1. *The effect of CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment temperature on microalgae fractionation and saccharification efficiency*

As shown in Fig. 6a, the lipid extraction rate increased significantly from 11.5 % to 20.8% after the pretreatment temperature increased from 80 °C to 120 °C. However, when the temperature increased from 120 °C to 140 °C, the fractionation efficiency of each component showed a slight downward trend. Lipid, protein, and monosaccharide decreased to 19.5%, 10.1 g/L, and 1.2 g/L, respec-tively. The involved reasons could be that lipids are easily degraded at high temperatures [39], and proteins and monosaccharides are more prone to undergo the Maillard reaction [40].

The significant increase in the saccharification rate was mainly attributed to the effective disintegration of the micro- algae cell wall, which significantly improved the accessibility of the enzyme. However, when the temperature continued to rise to 140 °C, the saccharification rate decreased rapidly from 87.6 % to 70.8 %.

3.3.2. The effect of CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment time on microalgae fractionation and saccharification efficiency The effect of time on CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment is shown in Fig. 6c. In the initial reaction time of 4 h, the lipid extraction rate was stable at about 20 %, while the protein and monosaccharide showed a rapid in- crease from 11.8 g/L to 15.0 g/L and 1.3 g/L to 1.9 g/L, respectively. It shows that DES has a more obvious solubilization effect on protein and monosaccharide than lipids in a short time. The optimal effect was achieved at 6 h, when the extraction rate of lipids was 27.1 %, and the concentrations of protein and monosaccharides in the solution were 16.5 g/L and 2.6 g/L, respectively. However, the yields of the three products showed a downward trend when the pretreatment time was prolonged. After 10 h, the lipid extraction rate decreased to 24.5 %, and the protein and monosaccharide concentrations decreased to 15.7 g/L and 2.1 g/L, respectively. It is worth noting that long-term high-tem- perature treatment more likely leads to protein hydrolysis into amino acids, acylation reaction with lipids, and Maillard reaction with carbo- hydrates [42].

In the enzymatic saccharification experiment of RMP, as the pre-treatment time increased to 6 h, the saccharification rate increased from 87.6 % (2 h) to 96.8 % (6 h), as shown in Fig. 6d, and decreased to 81.4 % and 76.6 % after 8 h and 10 h, respectively. The initial extension of time resulted in a complete lysis of microalgae cells, thereby increasing the saccharification rate. The longer time leads to the side reaction of the depolymerization product. Thus the toxic by-products inhibit the hydrolysis efficiency of the enzyme and reduce the saccharification rate.

3.4. _Lipid production from microalgae pretreated by the CC-LA-W0.5_ The ultimate goal of pretreatment is to use biomass components more efficiently. Therefore, the fermentation feasibility of DES aqueous phase and RMP enzymatic hydrolysate after CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment (120 °C for 6 h) was explored, as shown in Fig. 7.

### 3.4.1. Fermentation of DES aqueous phase by L. Starkeyi The aqueous phase of DES was diluted three times and used as a nutrient source to produce microbial lipids, mainly using proteins and small amounts of monosaccharides dissolved in DES. As shown in Fig. 7a, the lag phase of L. starkeyi was observed in the first 24 h, showing slow cell growth (a slight increase in DCW). Because of the DES system, the fermentation broth contains more or fewer fermentation inhibitors to inhibit cell growth, thus prolonging the lag phase of yeast [43]. In addition, the protein was almost not consumed during this period, mainly using monosaccharides, which was in line with the order

of microbial utilization of carbon sources (Reducing sugars present in the system were preferentially utilized by microorganisms) [44]. Subsequently, L. starkeyi entered the exponential growth phase, the cells grew rapidly and accumulated lipids and proteins, and monosaccharides were rapidly consumed. It is worth noting that monosaccharides were not detected at 36 h. Finally, 2.8 g/L DCW and 1.2 g/L microbial lipids were obtained after 72 h fermentation. This result indicates that the protein and a small amount of monosaccharides of microalgae are fractionated in the liquid phase after DES pretreatment, which can be efficiently utilized by biological fermentation.

3.4.2. Fermentation of RMP enzymatic hydrolysate by L. Starkeyi The enzymatic hydrolysate of RMP (solid loading of 5 %) was employed for L. starkeyi fermentation to produce microbial lipids, and the enzymatic hydrolysate of untreated microalgae was used as a control (CK). In Fig. 7b, the initial monosaccharide concentrations were 28.2 g/L (RMP) and 8.1 g/L (CK), respectively. This is preferred for the use of solid enzymatic hydrolysates as a carbon source, as no toxic inhibitors exist in the fermentation broth to ensure the normal growth of L. starkeyi. Therefore, it can be observed that there is almost no lag phase in the whole process, and the cells grow rapidly. In the first 12 h, the RMP (2.2 g/L DCW) group showed slower cell growth than the CK (2.8 g/L DCW) group. Because of the high concentration of monosaccharides in the fermentation broth of the RMP group, the cells need to adapt to the high-concentration environment for a while, thus stagnating growth resulting in a lower growth rate than the CK group. After 12 h, the cells in the RMP (4.2 g/L DCW) group proliferated, while the growth rate of the CK (3.2 g/L DCW) group slowed down, and there was almost no growth after 48 h. Because there were few monosaccharides left in the fermentation broth of the CK group after the first 12 h of fermentation, only 3.0 g/L monosaccharides were left, and the monosaccharides were exhausted after 48 h. Finally, after 72 h of fermentation, the monosaccharides in the RMP group were completely utilized by yeast. After 72 h, 10.7 g/L (RMP) and 4.3 g/L (CK) DCW, 5.3 g/L (RMP), and 1.5 g/L (CK) microbial lipids were obtained, respectively. These results demonstrate that the DES pretreatment can effectively improve the bioavailability of carbohydrates in microalgae.

3.7. Prospect of lipid production from microalgae biomass Microalgae have been used for many years as a source of value-added products with many commercial applications. The significant characteristics of microalgae biomass as a raw material for microbial culture include high carbohydrate content and lack of stubborn lignin [45,46]. Based on this, many studies have used microalgae biomass as fermentation raw materials to obtain more valuable microbial lipids (Table 3). For example, 3.6 g/L microbial lipid was obtained using the hydrolysate of Scenedesmus obtusiusculus as the fermentation carbon source [47]. Trichosporon oleaginosus obtained 6.8 g/L microbial lipids from the hydrolysate of P. oceanica [48]. The hydrolysate of Arthrospira platensis was fermented to obtain 9.6 g/L microbial lipids [49]. However, these biological pretreatment processes use expensive enzymatic combined treatment or chemical acid heat treatment. Although some have obtained considerable lipid yields, redundant detoxification steps, and high costs make it challenging to use microalgae biomass as a source of biofuels. Meanwhile, only carbohydrates are used, and most proteins are wasted.

In this study, the hydrolysate can be directly used for fermentation to obtain 6.5 g/L microbial lipids without additional detoxification steps. All components of microalgae biomass were fully utilized, and proteins and carbohydrates were converted into higher-quality microbial lipids (mainly palmitic acid, stearic acid, and oleic acid). This provides excellent help for the efficient utilization of microalgae biomass.

4. Conclusions A novel water-based DES pretreatment strategy was proposed to efficiently fractionate microalgae biomass and achieve full-component utilization of microalgae biomass. The CC-LA was illustrated to exhibit better pretreatment efficiency for more thoroughly breaking the microalgae cells, and a high saccharification rate of up to 83.2% was obtained. The specific surface area and crystallinity of CC-LA can be significantly improved by adding the appropriate amount of water. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the extraction rate of microalgae lipid reached 89.4%, and the saccharification rate of RMP achieved 96.8%. The protein and carbohydrate obtained by fraction-ation could be fermented to 8.9 g microbial lipid/100 g microalgae. The CC-LA-W0.5 prepared in this study is a new type of pretreatment solvent and can efficiently utilize each component of microalgae.

Fuel 363 (2024) 130892 <::logo: Elsevier NON SOLLUS An illustration of a person picking fruit from a tree with a banner that reads "NON SOLLUS" and the word "ELSEVIER" below::> Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Fuel journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/fuel <::logo: Elsevier FUEL the science and technology of fuel and energy ScienceDirect The logo features the word "FUEL" in large, bold, white letters with an orange outline, set against an orange background, with the Elsevier logo in the top left corner.::> <::logo: Check for updates A circular icon with a red and yellow ribbon, set against a blue background, above the text "Check for updates".::> Efficient fractionation of microalgae biomass as a whole for biodiesel production enabled by deep eutectic solvent and water Dayong Yu a,b, Hangyu Luo a,b, Jinyu Tan b, Junfa Yuan b, Jiasheng Chen b, Xiaofang Liu a,*, Hu Li b,* a Guizhou Provincial Key Laboratory for Rare Animal and Economic Insects of the Mountainous Region, College of Biology and Environmental Engineering, Guiyang University, Guiyang 550005, China b National Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide, Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide and Agricultural Bioengineering, Ministry of Education, State-Local Joint Laboratory for Comprehensive Utilization of Biomass, Center for R&D of Fine Chemicals, Guizhou University, Guiyang, 550025, China ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** Microalgae biomass Deep eutectic solvent Fractionation Microbial lipids ABSTRACT The fractionation of microalgae biomass and its efficient utilization have always been problems to be solved. Herein, microalgae biomass was pretreated with deep eutectic solvent (DES) to fractionate lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates, which were further converted into biodiesel. DES (CC-LA) synthesized from lactic acid and choline chloride had high fractionation efficiency, and the lipid extraction rate (17.7%) was 2.3 times higher than that of the untreated one (7.7%). Adding 0.5 mol water in CC-LA changed the polarity of the solvent, and the hydrogen bond acidity (α) and hydrogen bond alkalinity (β) increased from 1.37 and 0.52 to 1.42 and 0.54, respectively. Thus, the separation efficiency of DES was significantly improved. The lipid extraction rate was as high as 89.4%, the protein dissolution rate was as high as 84.2%, and the carbohydrate saccharification rate was as high as 96.8%. In addition, the isolated protein and glycosylated carbohydrates could be converted into 8.9 g microbial lipids/100 g microalgae biomass by *Lipomyces starkeyi*. The new water-promoted DES fractionation technology has dramatically enabled microalgae biomass's efficient and comprehensive utilization. # 1. Introduction Microalgae are unicellular organisms that are easy to culture, can efficiently fix CO2 and reproduce rapidly, and usually contain more than 80% organic matter, such as lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates [1]. These substances are high-quality sources for the preparation of biofuels. Therefore, microalgae are considered the new generation (third generation) of biomass raw materials for biofuel production [2,3]. Biofuels based on microalgae biomass mainly include bioethanol (fermentation of carbohydrates), biodiesel (transesterification of lipids), and biomethane (anaerobic fermentation) [4]. However, the utilization of microalgae biomass faces the problem of low efficiency. Because a large number of available substances are stored in the cytoplasm, the high resistance cell wall of microalgae hinders their effective utilization [5]. In addition, in most cases, only carbohydrates and lipids are used, and a large amount of protein is discharged as waste, resulting in a loss of overall biomass utilization [6]. To address this, it is crucial to develop an efficient and green pretreatment technique to efficiently pretreat and fractionate microalgae biomass (e.g., lipids, carbohydrates, and --- * Corresponding authors. Li). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fuel.2024.130892 Received 25 September 2023; Received in revised form 24 December 2023; Accepted 3 January 2024 Available online 16 January 2024 0016-2361/© 2024 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved. proteins), and the total biomass was converted into biodiesel to effi- ciently utilize microalgae biomass. The main technical problems for microalgae valorization are the destruction of the microalgae cell wall and the fractionation and utili- zation of total biomass. Currently, pretreatment methods include me- chanical pretreatment (e.g., milling, high-pressure homogenization, microwave, ultrasonication, and pulsed electric field), chemical pre- treatment (e.g., acid, alkali, organic soils, and oxidant), and biological pretreatment (e.g., enzymes and microorganisms) [7,8]. However, several problems are constantly encountered, such as high-energy con- sumption, corrosion of equipment, destruction of the environment, and inability to fractionate microalgae biomass effectively. It is necessary to explore a green and economical pretreatment/fractionation technology. Therefore, many new green solvents have been developed for pretreat- ment, such as ionic liquid (IL), liquid biphasic system (LBS), and deep eutectic solvent (DES). DES and IL have similar properties, such as non-flammable, non- volatile, recyclable, low vapor pressure, melting point, thermal stability, and so on [9]. However, compared with IL, DES has the advantages of Full Length Article D. Yu et al. Fuel 363 (2024) 130892 low cost, simple preparation, non-toxicity, and biodegradability, which makes it more promising [10]. LBS is used for the pretreatment of microalgae biomass, which has cost saving advantages, high separation efficiency, and protein invariance. However, the premise of its practical implementation is the need to destroy the cell wall of microalgae in advance [11]. Studies have shown that DES can effectively destroy the hydrogen bond network on the cell wall of microalgae to achieve the purpose of cracking microalgae cells. Meanwhile, DES has a high affinity for proteins and can quickly dissolve and extract a large number of proteins during the treatment of microalgae [12]. Significantly, the composition of DES can be freely adjusted to change its physicochemical properties. DES is hydrophilic, and adding an appropriate amount of water can reduce its viscosity and significantly improve its pretreatment performance [13,14]. It is, hence, an excellent choice to prepare suitable DES to pretreat fractionated microalgae biomass. Upon pretreatment of microalgae biomass with DES, lipids are con-verted into biodiesel by transesterification after extraction, and carbo-hydrates can be converted into biofuels by fermentation. Therefore, the fate of proteins dissolved in the DES phase must be considered. Lip-omyces starkeyi (L. starkeyi) is an excellent oleaginous yeast which pro-duces microbial lipids that can be converted into biodiesel by transesterification [15]. Notably, the substrates required for fermenta-tion are broad-spectrum, including reducing sugars, starch, lignocellu-losic hydrolysates, proteins, and fatty acids [16]. Therefore, the fractionated carbohydrates and proteins in the DES phase can be used as substrates for L. starkeyi to produce microbial lipids, thereby efficiently utilizing whole microalgae biomass. At the same time, it is necessary to consider the toxic effect of DES components on microorganisms during fermentation. Choline chloride-based DES has good biocompatibility and is widely used in biotransformation [17,18]. Therefore, choline chloride (CC) was used as a hydrogen bond acceptor to prepare different DESs in this paper. To fully utilize microalgae biomass, the concept of "full utilization" for producing biodiesel would be a promising strategy. In this work, a sustainable DES composed of CC and lactic acid (LA) with efficient pretreatment performance was screened out, and the effect of water on the pretreatment performance of the DES was explored. The influences of temperature and time on the optimal DES fractionation efficiency were investigated. After the reaction, the microalgae lipids were obtained by fractionation, and the proteins were fermented as substrates to convert into microbial lipids. The remaining solids (carbohydrates) were enzymatically hydrolyzed into monosaccharides as fermentation substrates, which were also converted into microbial lipids. Finally, the harvested microalgae lipids and microbial lipids were converted into biodiesel. The fractionation and "full utilization" of microalgae biomass components provide a good reference for upgrading biomass to biofuels or value-added chemicals. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Microalgae and chemicals Microalgae powder (_Nannochloropsis_ sp.) was purchased from Shandong Wudi Lvqi Biological Engineering Co., ltd. _Nannochloropsis_ sp. was dried at 105 °C for 48 h to calculate its water content. Carbohydrates, protein, and lipids of microalgae were determined by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL/TP-5100-60957) standard technique [19], Lowry method [20], and Bligh & Dyer method [21], respectively. The content of each component are water 10.5 ± 0.2 %, carbohydrate 15.3 ± 0.4 %, protein 39.2 ± 0.3 %, lipid 30.3 ± 0.6 %, and ash 11.1 ± 0.4 % respectively. The dried microalgae powder was stored in a sealed container and placed in a desiccator for later use. CC (≥99.0 %), formic acid (FA, ≥98.0 %), acetic acid (AA, ≥99.5 %), LA (≥99.0 %), and other chemicals of analytical purity grade were acquired from InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). ## 2.2. Dess synthesis and pretreatment Hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) (i.e., CC) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) (FA, AA, or LA) in a molar ratio of 1:2 were stirred at 80 °C and 600 rpm for 30 min to obtain a clear and transparent colorless liquid, denoted as CC-FA, CC-AA, and CC-LA [12]. For microalgae pretreatment in a typical procedure, CC-LA was added together with 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mol of water. Before use, the prepared DESs were stored in sealed containers and placed in a dryer to avoid absorbing moisture in the air. Typically, a mixture of 0.5 g microalgae powder and 10 g DES was placed in a pressure tube and heated at 600 rpm for pretreatment. The set heating temperature was 80, 100, 120, and 140 °C, and the required time was 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h. 2.3. Extraction of microalgae lipids and enzymatic hydrolysis of residual carbohydrates After pretreatment of microalgae with DES, 20 mL water was added to the reaction system, and then an equal volume of ethyl acetate was added to extract lipids. The upper ethyl acetate was harvested by centrifugation, and the above steps were repeated 3 times. The collected ethyl acetate was combined to remove the solvent by rotary evaporation, and the obtained microalgae lipids were placed at 105 °C to remove water and weighed to calculate the lipid extraction rate. The lipid extraction rate was determined by following the below equation: Lipid extraction rate (%) = $\frac{\text{Weight of lipid extracted}}{\text{Lipid weight in initial microalgae}}$ \times 100% (1) The DES aqueous phase was recovered to detect the content of monosaccharides and proteins and used for subsequent fermentation. The remaining solids were douched 3 times with double distilled water (ddH2O) to remove the residual DES and then dried at 105 °C to obtain the recovered microalgae powder (RMP) for subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis. The enzymatic hydrolysis reaction was evaluated under a 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 4.8) with a solid (raw and RMP) loading of 1% (w/v) and 20 FPU/g solid cellulase (Cellic® CTec2, Filter paper activity: 150 FPU/mL, Novozyme). A final concentration of 50 µg/mL tetracy- cline was then added to inhibit bacterial growth. The system was placed in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask and then hydrolyzed at 200 rpm for 12 h in a preheated (50 °C) shaker. The hydrolysate was taken out at intervals, and the concentration of monosaccharide was determined after the inactivation of the enzyme at 100 °C for 10 min. The concentrations of monosaccharide was detected by HPLC (Agilent 1260, Hi-Plex H, 300 × 7.7 mm, 8 µm) equipped with a differential refractive index detector (RID) with 0.05 mol/L dilute H2SO4 as the mobile phase (0.5 mL/min). The temperature of the column and RID was kept at 50 °C. The mono- saccharide yield was determined following the equation: Monosaccharide yield (%) = Monosaccharide in the enzymatic liquid (g) / Monosaccharide in the substrate (g) × 100% ## 2.4. Strain and cultivation Lipomyces starkeyi 2.2291 (L. starkeyi), supplied by China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center (CGMCC), was cultured on YPD (yeast peptone dextrose) medium (yeast extract: 10 g/L, tryptone: 20 g/L, glucose: 20 g/L and preparation of solid medium with additional agar: 20 g/L) and stored at 4 °C. The medium was sterilized in an autoclave at 115 °C for 20 min, and the glucose solution was sterilized alone. The general culture procedure of _L. starkeyi_ includes the following steps. (1) A pure culture of _L. starkeyi_ was obtained according to the 2 D. Yu et al. Fuel 363 (2024) 130892 activation procedure provided by CGMCC. (2) The pure culture was inoculated on a YPD solid plate, and a single colony was obtained after 48 h at 28 °C. (3) The single colony was inoculated in a YPD liquid medium, and the enriched pure culture was obtained after 24 h at 28 °C as the initial culture for fermentation. ## 2.5. Fermentation of DES aqueous phase after microalgae pretreatment To test the fermentability of the DES aqueous phase recovered after DES pretreatment of microalgae, L. starkeyi (microbial lipid production by fermentation) was used to evaluate the feasibility. The recovered DES aqueous phase was adjusted to pH 6.0 using solid NaOH, and then 0.5 g/ L MgSO4.7H2O and 1.0 g/L KH2PO4 were added. After sterilization at 121 °C for 20 min, it was used as a medium for L. starkeyi fermentation. The initial culture of L. starkeyi after YPD culture was centrifuged to discard the medium, and the cells were washed with sterile ddH2O 3 times and resuspended, followed by addition to the medium prepared with DES aqueous phase in an inoculation amount of 10% (v/v) so that the cell concentration in the initial fermentation broth was OD600 = 1.0 [22]. Subsequently, the fermentation system (in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask) was cultured in a shaker at 28 °C and 200 rpm for 72 h, and samples were taken every 12 h to determine the consumption of monosaccharides and proteins and the yield of dry cell weight (DCW) and microbial lipid. 2.6. Fermentation of RMP enzymatic hydrolysate To meet the high C/N ratio required for L. starkeyi fermentation, the solid loading for RMP hydrolysis was adjusted to 5 %. The hydrolysate obtained by replacing RMP with untreated, dry microalgae powder was used as a check (CK). 0.5 g/L MgSO4.7H2O, 1.0 g/L KH2PO4, and 0.22 g/ L (NH4)2SO4 were added to the obtained hydrolysate and then sterilized at 121 °C for 20 min and stored in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask. Subsequently, L. starkeyi was inoculated as described in Section 2.5 and fermented at 28 °C and 200 rpm for 72 h. Sampling was performed every 12 h to determine monosaccharide consumption (DCW) and microbial lipid production. 2.7. Lipid extraction After the fermentation broth was harvested, the wet cells were obtained by centrifugation, washed with ddH2O 3 times to remove the residual medium on the cell surface, and then freeze-dried to obtain dry cells. Lipid extraction was performed, according to the published literature [23]. The dry cells were resuspended with 4 M HCl to make the cell suspension concentration (0.1 g/mL). After standing at room temperature for 1 h, it was shaken well again and placed in a water bath at 100 °C for 10 min to lyse the cells fully. Then, an equal volume of methanol and 2 times chloroform were added, fully oscillated, and mixed for 30 min, followed by centrifuging at 8,000 rpm for 5 min. The chloroform layer was recovered, and the same volume of chloroform was added again, repeated 3 times. All chloroform was collected, and the solvent was removed by rotary evaporation. The obtained microbial lipid was dried to constant weight at 105 °C. DCW and lipid yield were determined using equations (3) and (4). DCW (g/L) = Weight of dried cell / Volume of fermentation medium (3) Lipid yield (g/L) = Weight of extracted lipid / Volume of fermentation medium 2.8. _Lipid transesterification and fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) composition analysis_ According to previous studies [24], a lipid transesterification reaction was completed in the methanol-sulfuric acid system. Typically, the extracted microalgae and microbial lipids were dissolved in methanol and transferred to a 15 mL pressure tube, then concentrated sulfuric acid was added to a final concentration of 2 % (w/w). The reaction system was placed at 80 °C for 2 h, and an equal volume of ddH2O and an equal volume of ethyl acetate were added to thoroughly mix. Subsequently, the composition of FAME was analyzed by GC-MS (Agilent 6890 N GC, 5973 MS) and GC (Agilent 7890B, HP-5 column: 30 m x 0.32 mm x 0.25 µm, and flame ionization detector) with SUPELCO standard mix as reference. 2.9. *Monosaccharides analytic* After pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and fermentation broth, the monosaccharides in DES aqueous phase were analyzed by HPLC (Agilent 1260, Hi-Plex H, 300 × 7.7 mm, 8 µm). The mobile phase was 50 mM H2SO4 (0.5 mL/min), the detector was RID, and the column temperature and detector temperature were set at 50 °C. 2.10. Characterization of DES and RMP 2.10.1. The scanning electron microscope analyzed raw material and RMP surface morphology (SEM, ZEISS SIGMA300). The N₂ adsorption-desorption isotherms of RMP were performed on a Micromeritics ASAP 2460 analyzer (196 °C) to measure the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area. Raw materials and RMP were recorded using X-ray diffraction (XRD) at 2θ degree of 10° to 80° using a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray powder diffractometer with Cu Kα (λ = 1.542 Å). Due to their relatively complete cell wall structure, the remaining solids in the untreated group resulted in only 6.9 g of carbohydrates produced during the enzymatic hydrolysis process. In the solid part, the cell wall was fully broken, which was conducive to the enzyme hydrolysis, and 9.8 g of carbohydrate was obtained. Prospect of lipid production from microalgae biomass Microalgae have been used for many years as a source of value-added products with many commercial applications. The significant characteristics of microalgae biomass as a raw material for microbial culture include high carbohydrate content and lack of stubborn lignin [45,46]. Based on this, many studies have used microalgae biomass as fermentation raw materials to obtain more valuable microbial lipids (Table 3). For example, 3.6 g/L microbial lipid was obtained using the hydrolysate of Scenedesmus obtusiusculus as the fermentation carbon source [47]. Trichosporon oleaginosus obtained 6.8 g/L microbial lipids from the hydrolysate of P. oceanica [48]. The hydrolysate of Arthrospira platensis was fermented to obtain 9.6 g/L microbial lipids [49]. However, these biological pretreatment processes use expensive enzymatic combined treatment or chemical acid heat treatment. Although some have obtained considerable lipid yields, redundant detoxification steps, and high costs make it challenging to use microalgae biomass as a source of biofuels. Meanwhile, only carbohydrates are used, and most proteins are wasted. In this study, the hydrolysate can be directly used for fermentation to obtain 6.5 g/L microbial lipids without additional detoxification steps. All components of microalgae biomass were fully utilized, and proteins and carbohydrates were converted into higher-quality microbial lipids (mainly palmitic acid, stearic acid, and oleic acid). This provides excellent help for the efficient utilization of microalgae biomass. 4. Conclusions A novel water-based DES pretreatment strategy was proposed to efficiently fractionate microalgae biomass and achieve full-component utilization of microalgae biomass. The CC-LA was illustrated to exhibit better pretreatment efficiency for more thoroughly breaking the microalgae cells, and a high saccharification rate of up to 83.2% was obtained. The specific surface area and crystallinity of CC-LA can be significantly improved by adding the appropriate amount of water. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the extraction rate of microalgae lipid reached 89.4%, and the saccharification rate of RMP achieved 96.8%. The protein and carbohydrate obtained by fraction-ation could be fermented to 8.9 g microbial lipid/100 g microalgae. The CC-LA-W0.5 prepared in this study is a new type of pretreatment solvent and can efficiently utilize each component of microalgae. Herein, microalgae biomass was pretreated with deep eutectic solvent (DES) to fractionate lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates, which were further converted into biodiesel. DES (CC-LA) synthesized from lactic acid and choline chloride had high fractionation efficiency, and the lipid extraction rate (17.7%) was 2.3 times higher than that of the untreated one (7.7%). Adding 0.5 mol water in CC-LA changed the polarity of the solvent, and the hydrogen bond acidity (α) and hydrogen bond alkalinity (β) increased from 1.37 and 0.52 to 1.42 and 0.54, respectively. Thus, the separation efficiency of DES was significantly improved. The lipid extraction rate was as high as 89.4%, the protein dissolution rate was as high as 84.2%, and the carbohydrate saccharification rate was as high as 96.8%. Introduction Microalgae are unicellular organisms that are easy to culture, can efficiently fix CO2 and reproduce rapidly, and usually contain more than 80% organic matter, such as lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates [1]. These substances are high-quality sources for the preparation of biofuels. Therefore, microalgae are considered the new generation (third generation) of biomass raw materials for biofuel production [2,3]. Biofuels based on microalgae biomass mainly include bioethanol (fermentation of carbohydrates), biodiesel (transesterification of lipids), and biomethane (anaerobic fermentation) [4]. However, the utilization of microalgae biomass faces the problem of low efficiency. Because a large number of available substances are stored in the cytoplasm, the high resistance cell wall of microalgae hinders their effective utilization [5]. In addition, in most cases, only carbohydrates and lipids are used, and a large amount of protein is discharged as waste, resulting in a loss of overall biomass utilization [6]. To address this, it is crucial to develop an efficient and green pretreatment technique to efficiently pretreat and fractionate microalgae biomass (e.g., lipids, carbohydrates, and --- * Corresponding authors. All rights reserved. proteins), and the total biomass was converted into biodiesel to effi- ciently utilize microalgae biomass. The main technical problems for microalgae valorization are the destruction of the microalgae cell wall and the fractionation and utili- zation of total biomass. Currently, pretreatment methods include me- chanical pretreatment (e.g., milling, high-pressure homogenization, microwave, ultrasonication, and pulsed electric field), chemical pre- treatment (e.g., acid, alkali, organic soils, and oxidant), and biological pretreatment (e.g., enzymes and microorganisms) [7,8]. However, several problems are constantly encountered, such as high-energy con- sumption, corrosion of equipment, destruction of the environment, and inability to fractionate microalgae biomass effectively. It is necessary to explore a green and economical pretreatment/fractionation technology. Therefore, many new green solvents have been developed for pretreat- ment, such as ionic liquid (IL), liquid biphasic system (LBS), and deep eutectic solvent (DES). DES and IL have similar properties, such as non-flammable, non- volatile, recyclable, low vapor pressure, melting point, thermal stability, and so on [9]. However, compared with IL, DES has the advantages of Full Length Article D. Yu et al. Fuel 363 (2024) 130892 low cost, simple preparation, non-toxicity, and biodegradability, which makes it more promising [10]. LBS is used for the pretreatment of microalgae biomass, which has cost saving advantages, high separation efficiency, and protein invariance. However, the premise of its practical implementation is the need to destroy the cell wall of microalgae in advance [11]. Studies have shown that DES can effectively destroy the hydrogen bond network on the cell wall of microalgae to achieve the purpose of cracking microalgae cells. Meanwhile, DES has a high affinity for proteins and can quickly dissolve and extract a large number of proteins during the treatment of microalgae [12]. Significantly, the composition of DES can be freely adjusted to change its physicochemical properties. DES is hydrophilic, and adding an appropriate amount of water can reduce its viscosity and significantly improve its pretreatment performance [13,14]. It is, hence, an excellent choice to prepare suitable DES to pretreat fractionated microalgae biomass. Upon pretreatment of microalgae biomass with DES, lipids are con-verted into biodiesel by transesterification after extraction, and carbo-hydrates can be converted into biofuels by fermentation. Therefore, the fate of proteins dissolved in the DES phase must be considered. Lip-omyces starkeyi (L. starkeyi) is an excellent oleaginous yeast which pro-duces microbial lipids that can be converted into biodiesel by transesterification [15]. Notably, the substrates required for fermenta-tion are broad-spectrum, including reducing sugars, starch, lignocellu-losic hydrolysates, proteins, and fatty acids [16]. Therefore, the fractionated carbohydrates and proteins in the DES phase can be used as substrates for L. starkeyi to produce microbial lipids, thereby efficiently utilizing whole microalgae biomass. At the same time, it is necessary to consider the toxic effect of DES components on microorganisms during fermentation. Choline chloride-based DES has good biocompatibility and is widely used in biotransformation [17,18]. Therefore, choline chloride (CC) was used as a hydrogen bond acceptor to prepare different DESs in this paper. To fully utilize microalgae biomass, the concept of "full utilization" for producing biodiesel would be a promising strategy. In this work, a sustainable DES composed of CC and lactic acid (LA) with efficient pretreatment performance was screened out, and the effect of water on the pretreatment performance of the DES was explored. The influences of temperature and time on the optimal DES fractionation efficiency were investigated. After the reaction, the microalgae lipids were obtained by fractionation, and the proteins were fermented as substrates to convert into microbial lipids. The remaining solids (carbohydrates) were enzymatically hydrolyzed into monosaccharides as fermentation substrates, which were also converted into microbial lipids. Finally, the harvested microalgae lipids and microbial lipids were converted into biodiesel. The fractionation and "full utilization" of microalgae biomass components provide a good reference for upgrading biomass to biofuels or value-added chemicals. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Microalgae and chemicals Microalgae powder (_Nannochloropsis_ sp.) was purchased from Shandong Wudi Lvqi Biological Engineering Co., ltd. _Nannochloropsis_ sp. was dried at 105 °C for 48 h to calculate its water content. Carbohydrates, protein, and lipids of microalgae were determined by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL/TP-5100-60957) standard technique [19], Lowry method [20], and Bligh & Dyer method [21], respectively. The content of each component are water 10.5 ± 0.2 %, carbohydrate 15.3 ± 0.4 %, protein 39.2 ± 0.3 %, lipid 30.3 ± 0.6 %, and ash 11.1 ± 0.4 % respectively. The dried microalgae powder was stored in a sealed container and placed in a desiccator for later use. CC (≥99.0 %), formic acid (FA, ≥98.0 %), acetic acid (AA, ≥99.5 %), LA (≥99.0 %), and other chemicals of analytical purity grade were acquired from InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). ## 2.2. Dess synthesis and pretreatment Hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) (i.e., CC) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) (FA, AA, or LA) in a molar ratio of 1:2 were stirred at 80 °C and 600 rpm for 30 min to obtain a clear and transparent colorless liquid, denoted as CC-FA, CC-AA, and CC-LA [12]. For microalgae pretreatment in a typical procedure, CC-LA was added together with 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mol of water. Before use, the prepared DESs were stored in sealed containers and placed in a dryer to avoid absorbing moisture in the air. Typically, a mixture of 0.5 g microalgae powder and 10 g DES was placed in a pressure tube and heated at 600 rpm for pretreatment. The set heating temperature was 80, 100, 120, and 140 °C, and the required time was 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 h. 2.3. Extraction of microalgae lipids and enzymatic hydrolysis of residual carbohydrates After pretreatment of microalgae with DES, 20 mL water was added to the reaction system, and then an equal volume of ethyl acetate was added to extract lipids. The upper ethyl acetate was harvested by centrifugation, and the above steps were repeated 3 times. The collected ethyl acetate was combined to remove the solvent by rotary evaporation, and the obtained microalgae lipids were placed at 105 °C to remove water and weighed to calculate the lipid extraction rate. The lipid extraction rate was determined by following the below equation: Lipid extraction rate (%) = $\frac{\text{Weight of lipid extracted}}{\text{Lipid weight in initial microalgae}}$ \times 100% (1) The DES aqueous phase was recovered to detect the content of monosaccharides and proteins and used for subsequent fermentation. The remaining solids were douched 3 times with double distilled water (ddH2O) to remove the residual DES and then dried at 105 °C to obtain the recovered microalgae powder (RMP) for subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis. The enzymatic hydrolysis reaction was evaluated under a 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 4.8) with a solid (raw and RMP) loading of 1% (w/v) and 20 FPU/g solid cellulase (Cellic® CTec2, Filter paper activity: 150 FPU/mL, Novozyme). A final concentration of 50 µg/mL tetracy- cline was then added to inhibit bacterial growth. The system was placed in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask and then hydrolyzed at 200 rpm for 12 h in a preheated (50 °C) shaker. The hydrolysate was taken out at intervals, and the concentration of monosaccharide was determined after the inactivation of the enzyme at 100 °C for 10 min. The concentrations of monosaccharide was detected by HPLC (Agilent 1260, Hi-Plex H, 300 × 7.7 mm, 8 µm) equipped with a differential refractive index detector (RID) with 0.05 mol/L dilute H2SO4 as the mobile phase (0.5 mL/min). The temperature of the column and RID was kept at 50 °C. The mono- saccharide yield was determined following the equation: Monosaccharide yield (%) = Monosaccharide in the enzymatic liquid (g) / Monosaccharide in the substrate (g) × 100% ## 2.4. Strain and cultivation Lipomyces starkeyi 2.2291 (L. starkeyi), supplied by China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center (CGMCC), was cultured on YPD (yeast peptone dextrose) medium (yeast extract: 10 g/L, tryptone: 20 g/L, glucose: 20 g/L and preparation of solid medium with additional agar: 20 g/L) and stored at 4 °C. The medium was sterilized in an autoclave at 115 °C for 20 min, and the glucose solution was sterilized alone. The general culture procedure of _L. starkeyi_ includes the following steps. (1) A pure culture of _L. starkeyi_ was obtained according to the 2 D. Yu et al. Fuel 363 (2024) 130892 activation procedure provided by CGMCC. (2) The pure culture was inoculated on a YPD solid plate, and a single colony was obtained after 48 h at 28 °C. (3) The single colony was inoculated in a YPD liquid medium, and the enriched pure culture was obtained after 24 h at 28 °C as the initial culture for fermentation. ## 2.5. Fermentation of DES aqueous phase after microalgae pretreatment To test the fermentability of the DES aqueous phase recovered after DES pretreatment of microalgae, L. starkeyi (microbial lipid production by fermentation) was used to evaluate the feasibility. The recovered DES aqueous phase was adjusted to pH 6.0 using solid NaOH, and then 0.5 g/ L MgSO4.7H2O and 1.0 g/L KH2PO4 were added. After sterilization at 121 °C for 20 min, it was used as a medium for L. starkeyi fermentation. Therefore, the fermentation feasibility of DES aqueous phase and RMP enzymatic hydrolysate after CC-LA-W0.5 pretreatment (120 °C for 6 h) was explored, as shown in Fig. 7. ### 3.4.1. Fermentation of DES aqueous phase by L. Starkeyi The aqueous phase of DES was diluted three times and used as a nutrient source to produce microbial lipids, mainly using proteins and small amounts of monosaccharides dissolved in DES. As shown in Fig. 7a, the lag phase of L. starkeyi was observed in the first 24 h, showing slow cell growth (a slight increase in DCW). Because of the DES system, the fermentation broth contains more or fewer fermentation inhibitors to inhibit cell growth, thus prolonging the lag phase of yeast [43]. In addition, the protein was almost not consumed during this period, mainly using monosaccharides, which was in line with the order of microbial utilization of carbon sources (Reducing sugars present in the system were preferentially utilized by microorganisms) [44]. Subsequently, L. starkeyi entered the exponential growth phase, the cells grew rapidly and accumulated lipids and proteins, and monosaccharides were rapidly consumed. It is worth noting that monosaccharides were not detected at 36 h. Finally, 2.8 g/L DCW and 1.2 g/L microbial lipids were obtained after 72 h fermentation. This result indicates that the protein and a small amount of monosaccharides of microalgae are fractionated in the liquid phase after DES pretreatment, which can be efficiently utilized by biological fermentation. 3.4.2. Fermentation of RMP enzymatic hydrolysate by L. Starkeyi The enzymatic hydrolysate of RMP (solid loading of 5 %) was employed for L. starkeyi fermentation to produce microbial lipids, and the enzymatic hydrolysate of untreated microalgae was used as a control (CK). In Fig. 7b, the initial monosaccharide concentrations were 28.2 g/L (RMP) and 8.1 g/L (CK), respectively. This is preferred for the use of solid enzymatic hydrolysates as a carbon source, as no toxic inhibitors exist in the fermentation broth to ensure the normal growth of L. starkeyi. Therefore, it can be observed that there is almost no lag phase in the whole process, and the cells grow rapidly. In the first 12 h, the RMP (2.2 g/L DCW) group showed slower cell growth than the CK (2.8 g/L DCW) group. Because of the high concentration of monosaccharides in the fermentation broth of the RMP group, the cells need to adapt to the high-concentration environment for a while, thus stagnating growth resulting in a lower growth rate than the CK group. After 12 h, the cells in the RMP (4.2 g/L DCW) group proliferated, while the growth rate of the CK (3.2 g/L DCW) group slowed down, and there was almost no growth after 48 h. Because there were few monosaccharides left in the fermentation broth of the CK group after the first 12 h of fermentation, only 3.0 g/L monosaccharides were left, and the monosaccharides were exhausted after 48 h. Finally, after 72 h of fermentation, the monosaccharides in the RMP group were completely utilized by yeast. After 72 h, 10.7 g/L (RMP) and 4.3 g/L (CK) DCW, 5.3 g/L (RMP), and 1.5 g/L (CK) microbial lipids were obtained, respectively. Prospect of lipid production from microalgae biomass Microalgae have been used for many years as a source of value-added products with many commercial applications. The significant characteristics of microalgae biomass as a raw material for microbial culture include high carbohydrate content and lack of stubborn lignin [45,46]. Based on this, many studies have used microalgae biomass as fermentation raw materials to obtain more valuable microbial lipids (Table 3). For example, 3.6 g/L microbial lipid was obtained using the hydrolysate of Scenedesmus obtusiusculus as the fermentation carbon source [47]. Trichosporon oleaginosus obtained 6.8 g/L microbial lipids from the hydrolysate of P. oceanica [48]. The hydrolysate of Arthrospira platensis was fermented to obtain 9.6 g/L microbial lipids [49]. However, these biological pretreatment processes use expensive enzymatic combined treatment or chemical acid heat treatment. Although some have obtained considerable lipid yields, redundant detoxification steps, and high costs make it challenging to use microalgae biomass as a source of biofuels. Meanwhile, only carbohydrates are used, and most proteins are wasted. In this study, the hydrolysate can be directly used for fermentation to obtain 6.5 g/L microbial lipids without additional detoxification steps. All components of microalgae biomass were fully utilized, and proteins and carbohydrates were converted into higher-quality microbial lipids (mainly palmitic acid, stearic acid, and oleic acid). This provides excellent help for the efficient utilization of microalgae biomass. 4. Conclusions A novel water-based DES pretreatment strategy was proposed to efficiently fractionate microalgae biomass and achieve full-component utilization of microalgae biomass. The CC-LA was illustrated to exhibit better pretreatment efficiency for more thoroughly breaking the microalgae cells, and a high saccharification rate of up to 83.2% was obtained. The specific surface area and crystallinity of CC-LA can be significantly improved by adding the appropriate amount of water. Under the optimal pretreatment conditions, the extraction rate of microalgae lipid reached 89.4%, and the saccharification rate of RMP achieved 96.8%. The protein and carbohydrate obtained by fraction-ation could be fermented to 8.9 g microbial lipid/100 g microalgae. The CC-LA-W0.5 prepared in this study is a new type of pretreatment solvent and can efficiently utilize each component of microalgae.
